translation:
M. Tsani V

The Holy Community of Lukow B

The ancient community in Lukow B was situated, geographically and strategically, at a noisy crossroads between Poland and Lithuania, and ruled over the district of Podlasie. Therefore, perhaps Lukow B was the oldest Jewish settlement in Podlasie. Before the Christians established a church, the Jews there established their own synagogue. If the city did not appear in the accounts of the stormy campaigns of the bands of Chmielnicki, the Swedes, Napoleon’s army, the Russians, and others, that is only because the passersby robbed, murdered, and burned everything so thoroughly that no trace remained for those who came afterward. As stormy as the history of the crown city was, so stormy and full of life was the Jewish life of Lukow. The holy community of Lukow had great lineage; it had the important rabbis of Podlasie, and its last rabbi, if I am not mistaken, was a grandson of the Kotzker.

Just as the flame of Kotzk Hasidism burned in all its colors, so later, until the Holocaust, the flame of the vision of nationalism and social liberation burned—at least for the entire world. The Jews of Lukow were of Podlasian stock: healthy, industrious, honest, and not a few conservative. In the war between the Mitnagdim and the Hasidim, the Jews of Lukow fought like lions against Hasidism; but once they had tasted the flavor of Hasidism, not even a single opponent of it remained in Lukow. Thus, too, in modern times the Jews of Lukow knew no compromises—immersed in everything: immersed in Zionism, immersed in Bundism, and if revolution, then a worldwide one, such as would not leave even the most distant village anywhere in Asia…
translatorNotes: The opening “מ. צאני ו” and heading “ק״ק לוקו ב” are preserved as rendered from the OCR; their exact intended forms are uncertain.
“חזו ן לאומ י ושחרו ר סוציאל י” is translated literally as “the vision of nationalism and social liberation”; the wording may reflect ambiguous OCR or an unusual historical formulation.
“הכתר” literally means “the crown”; “crown city” preserves that wording without resolving its historical reference.
“הקוצקאי” means “the Kotzker,” referring to the Hasidic tradition or figure associated with Kotzk.
